newsitem.title: USA: CBOT grain delivery change may hit small elevators.
newsitem.headline: CBOT grain delivery change may hit small elevators.

text.p: A proposal to drastically change the Chicago Board of Trade corn and soybean delivery system will likely pass a membership vote next month but analysts and brokers said it might hurt small river elevators.

"If they just license the big names as deliverable points (along the Illinois River) it's going to affect elevators next to deliverable points," said one Chicago-based commercial grain broker, who like others asked anonymity on the issue.
"Farmers will work directly with the processor or the big grain houses and the smaller guys will lose out," he added.

The exchange's proposal, drawn up by a CBOT-appointed Grain Delivery Task Force, would eliminate Toledo and St. Louis as delivery locations and make the sole delivery sites as elevators located on the Illinois River between Pekin, Ill., and Chicago, including Burns Harbor, Ind.
CBOT members will vote on April 15 whether to change the delivery system. The Board passed the change on March 4.

The Task Force was established after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in December told the CBOT that delivery terms of its corn and soybean contracts were no longer suitable due to changes in cash grain marketing.

The CFTC said reduced amounts of physical grain storage, notably in Chicago, along with large increases in speculative open interest in grain futures, required changes in the traditional delivery of cash against CBOT futures.
David Lehman, CBOT group manager, commodity products, said the CBOT proposal would increase grain capacity to 161 million bushels from 70 million bushels currently available.
CFTC said it would make its own recommendations if CBOT failed to come up with a solution and last week opened a period of public comment on the CBOT's proposed changes.
That is because the CBOT proposal requires the new Illinois river elevator locations have a minimum $2 million working capital and $40 million net worth to qualify.
CBOT's Lehman said the minimum net worth requirement could price at least six smaller elevators out of contention unless they team up with other firms with more capital, he said.
"The reason for increasing the net worth requirement is based on recognizing shipping certificates are not the same as warehouse receipts," he said.
"There are six (firms) we don't know whether they would meet the financial requirements," Lehman added.
Lehman noted the current system guaranteed takers of delivery would have the grain. Shipping certificates give the taker only the right to receive the grain, not a guarantee.
Several task force members downplayed the issue, saying the proposal would eliminate current advantages for delivery.

"If the (current) contract is poorly drawn so that it has a bias, it will be highly desirable for one party (to deliver) and not desirable at all for the other party," said one task force member, who asked not to be named.
"The goal obviously was to put forward a contract that would reflect a balance between those two interests."

He said the proposal balanced the needs of the three primary users of grain -- exporters, processors and livestock feeders. The Illinois location put the supplies at the center of production and usage, he said.
Most analysts said eliminating St. Louis as a delivery location would have little effect on the market because very little grain was registered for delivery there.
Eliminating Toledo was a touchier issue, they said. Toledo has been a prime delivery location for corn and soybeans as the main access point for the St. Lawrence Seaway.
"I'm a little bit surprised they would think about getting rid of Toledo," one grain analyst said. "That restricts access to the St. Lawrence Seaway."
But the task force member said the Illinois River location was in the center of production and usage and better reflected the commodity's true price.

"It has nothing to do with capacity, it has everything to do with geography," the member said. "The (proposed) contract correlates to the activities that are in its own back yard instead of the eastern perimeter of the eastern corn belt."
